title: Fabric choice for blackwork
subtitle: Count and colour: two decisions before you buy cloth
excerpt: Blackwork needs evenweave fabric so the stitches sit at even distances from each other. The fabric count determines the finished size; the fabric colour frames the black thread. Both decisions are made before you cut your cloth.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s to 1900s), blackwork sampler chapters.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fabric woven with the same number of threads per centimetre in both directions. Blackwork is counted over these even intersections.
The number of threads per inch in each direction. Higher count means smaller stitches and finer detail.
Linen woven at 28 threads per inch. A standard choice for blackwork, giving a finished stitch size of roughly 1 mm each.

content.text: Blackwork is a counted stitch, so the

fabric must have the same thread count in both directions. Warp and weft at different counts produce distorted stitches; the diagonal fills in fill patterns look wrong, and outlines that should be square end up as rectangles.

determines how large your finished stitches are. A 25-count cloth gives stitches roughly 1 mm across when worked over one thread. A 28-count cloth gives slightly smaller stitches. A 32-count cloth is fine work best seen under daylight.
is a reasonable starting point. The stitches are clear enough to count without magnification, and two strands of stranded cotton fill the holes without puckering.

Traditional blackwork uses black thread on white or cream cloth. The contrast lets the pattern read clearly. Antique linen has a warm cream tone that softens the black thread; bleached white linen gives a sharper, more graphic result.

Modern blackwork sometimes uses charcoal thread on coloured cloth, or dark red or navy on cream. These work well as long as there is strong contrast between thread and ground. A 50 per cent mid-tone ground with a mid-tone thread will produce a flat, hard-to-read result.
Cut the cloth several centimetres larger than the finished design on all sides. You need working room around the stitched area for mounting in the hoop.
Oversew or tape the raw edges to prevent fraying during stitching. A zigzag stitch by machine works well; a whip stitch by hand is slower but equally effective.
Fold and press lightly to find the centre. Mark it with a pin or a tacking thread. This becomes your starting point when you are following
Mount in a hoop. Blackwork worked in the hand tends to pull unevenly; the hoop keeps consistent tension.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: Fabric-related issues that show up early.

items.symptom: Stitches look uneven in one direction
items.cause: The fabric is not a true evenweave; warp and weft thread counts differ.
items.fix: Count threads along both axes before cutting. If the counts differ, choose a different fabric.

items.cause: Using too many strands for the fabric count.
items.fix: On 28-count, two strands of stranded cotton is standard. On 32-count, drop to one strand.
